strengths: Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art RD performance (BD-rate -15.91%/-21.34%/-17.58% vs. VTM-21.0 on Kodak/Tecnick/CLIC) with comparisons against a comprehensive set of recent baselines, including both transformer-based and Mamba-based LIC models.

Favorable complexity-performance trade-off: the paper reports parameters, FLOPs, decoding latency, and peak memory on 2K images, showing clear efficiency advantages over prior Mamba-based models (e.g., 57% less GPU memory than MambaIC), which strengthens the practical significance of the contribution.

Reasonably thorough evaluation: component ablations (CTA, GPP), structural ablations against Conv/Swin/window-attention/vanilla-Mamba blocks at matched parameter counts, ERF visualization, and cluster visualizations provide multi-faceted evidence that the proposed modules, not just overall architecture scale, drive the gains.

The identified problems of vanilla Mamba for 2D image data (content-agnostic fixed scans, strict causality, long-range decay) are clearly motivated, and the content-adaptive reordering idea is a sensible, linear-complexity remedy.
The paper is generally well written and organized, with a clear problem statement, method description, and honest limitations section.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: both components are close adaptations of existing techniques — the token reordering/re-grouping idea has appeared in prior scan-reordering work, and the prompt-conditioned output kernel directly follows the Attentive State-Space Model of MambaIRv2 (Guo et al., 2024a), as the authors themselves acknowledge. The paper reads more as a well-engineered application of these ideas to LIC than a fundamentally new method.

The claim that prompt conditioning 'relaxes strict causality' and lets the model 'query information from unscanned tokens' is technically overstated. Adding a per-cluster dictionary vector to C modulates the readout of the hidden state but provides no access to future tokens' features; it injects static, learned cluster priors, not future context. A more precise characterization or analysis of what the prompts actually encode is missing.

Some important design choices lack ablation: the number of clusters K is fixed at 64 with no sensitivity analysis, and there is no ablation on K-Means iterations T, EMA decay, or the effect of cluster assignment instability at inference (train-time iterative updates vs. test-time single assignment).

No theoretical or quantitative analysis of the trade-off introduced by destroying spatial locality in the scan order (clustering by feature similarity makes the 1-D sequence spatially incoherent); the paper asserts this is beneficial but only provides qualitative visual evidence.

No code or checkpoints are released at submission time (promised upon acceptance), which weakens reproducibility; the reproduction of MambaIC was conducted by the authors themselves rather than using official results, introducing potential bias in the closest-baseline comparison.

Minor presentation issues (e.g., 'Rate ravings', 'Tecknick') and a heuristic entropy-model modification (depthwise conv + gated MLP) that is described only briefly and deferred to supplementary material.

strengths: The paper targets a well-motivated and timely problem: adapting causal, content-agnostic selective scans in Mamba to the non-causal, content-dependent nature of 2D images for learned image compression.

Comprehensive rate-distortion evaluation on three standard benchmarks (Kodak, Tecnick, CLIC) against many recent strong baselines including VTM-21.0, FTIC, MLIC++, CCA, and two Mamba-based LIC models, with competitive BD-rate results (-15.91% to -21.34%).
Complexity analysis is included (params, FLOPs, decoding latency, peak memory), showing a favorable complexity-performance trade-off relative to prior Mamba-based LIC models.

Component ablations (Table 2) and structure ablations (Table 3) support the contribution of each proposed component, and ERF and cluster visualizations provide qualitative evidence for the intended mechanism.
Writing and overall structure are clear, and the limitations section is candid about the lack of enforced ordering across/within clusters.
weaknesses: The claim that prompt conditioning 'relaxes the strict causality' and lets the model 'query information from unscanned tokens' is conceptually overclaimed and not substantiated. In a causal selective scan, the hidden state h_i only aggregates past tokens; augmenting the output matrix (C+P) can only modulate how past state is read out, not access future tokens. No analysis or experiment convincingly demonstrates that this mechanism actually mitigates causality or long-range decay, despite this being a core motivation.

A critical soundness issue for a compression system is not addressed: the token reordering permutation is derived from feature-based clustering. It is unclear whether cluster assignments at encoding time are computed from the latent y or the quantized y_hat, and whether the decoder can reproduce the exact same permutation without side information. Any encoder/decoder mismatch in cluster assignments or cluster centers would break the transform at the decoder; the paper should explicitly prove decoder-side consistency (or entropy-code the assignments) and report the associated overhead.

Novelty is incremental. The prompt-augmented output matrix directly follows the Attentive State-Space design of MambaIRv2 (Guo et al.), and feature-based token reordering/reorganization for Mamba has been explored in prior vision works; the prompt dictionary (P = ΓD, a one-hot lookup added to C) is a simple mechanism. The main contribution amounts to combining known ideas in an LIC pipeline.

The evaluation confounds the proposed CAM blocks with entropy-model modifications (depthwise convolution and gated MLP additions to SCCTX). The main gains may partly stem from the modified entropy model rather than CAM itself; a cleaner ablation isolating the entropy-model changes is missing.

Missing ablations on key hyperparameters: sensitivity to the number of clusters K=64, the number of K-Means iterations T, EMA decay, and the training/inference cost of clustering at 2K resolution (is the 5% overhead figure measured for training only? Does clustering latency appear in the reported decoding latency and FLOPs?).

Baseline comparability is imperfect: complexity numbers are reported for models of very different scales (33M–157M params), MambaIC is only a self-conducted reproduction (no official code), and the MS-SSIM comparison is limited to a single dataset (CLIC). BD-PSNR gains over FTIC (0.15–0.36 dB) are modest relative to the headline BD-rate figures, and the text inconsistently orders datasets ('Kodak, CLIC, and Tecnick') versus the convention used elsewhere, raising questions of care.

Statistical significance is not addressed: BD-rate is computed over only 24–30 test images with no variance or significance analysis, and the checklist claim that error bars are unnecessary is not justified. Code is not released at submission time (only promised upon acceptance), which weakens reproducibility given the intricate clustering/reordering pipeline.

Some writing/presentation issues: typos in Figure 1 ('Rate ravings', 'Tecknick'), missing period in Section 4.4 ('scans This favorable...'), and the checklist answers several items as 'Yes' (e.g., theory, statistical significance) without corresponding evidence in the paper.

strengths: Strong empirical results: CMIC achieves state-of-the-art BD-rate over VTM-21.0 (-15.91%, -21.34%, -17.58% on Kodak, Tecnick, CLIC) and clearly outperforms prior Mamba-based LIC models (MambaVC, MambaIC) across the entire bitrate range.

Good complexity-performance trade-off: with only 69.11M parameters, the model beats much larger competitors (MambaIC at 157M, MLIC++ at 116M), with reasonable FLOPs, latency, and memory; the single-selective-scan design avoids the cost of multi-directional 2D scans.

The paper is well motivated: it identifies two concrete, plausible limitations of applying vanilla Mamba to images (content-agnostic fixed scans; strict causality and long-range decay), and each proposed component (CTA, GPP) directly targets one of them.

Reasonably thorough ablations: component-wise ablation (Table 2) isolates the contribution of each module, block-structure comparison (Table 3) validates CAM over conv/attention/standard-Mamba alternatives at matched parameter counts, plus ERF visualization and qualitative cluster visualizations that support the mechanism claims.
Clear writing and good positioning within both the LIC and SSM literature; limitations and future work are explicitly discussed.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: both key ideas are adapted from existing work - content-similarity-based token reordering is closely related to MambaIRv2's attentive state-space mechanism (which the authors themselves build upon for prompt conditioning), and learnable prompt dictionaries are a standard technique. The contribution is largely a well-engineered combination applied to LIC rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The claim that prompt conditioning 'relaxes strict causality' is under-theorized. Modulating the output matrix C with per-token prompts gives readout access to the hidden state but does not change the strictly causal state recurrence; a more precise characterization of what information the model can actually access (and why it helps) would strengthen the technical contribution.

Evaluation concerns: (i) MambaIC results come from the authors' own reproduction since official code is unavailable, introducing potential bias; (ii) comparisons are not fully controlled - e.g., CMIC uses the SCCTX entropy model while some baselines use stronger entropy models, making it hard to attribute gains solely to the transform; (iii) no error bars or multiple training runs to assess variance.

Some methodological details are missing or relegated to supplementary material: how clustering interacts with the non-differentiable K-means assignment (gradient flow through the reordering), behavior of clustering at inference on unseen content, sensitivity to the number of clusters K, and how the prompts interact with multi-scale stages.

No code or checkpoint release at submission time ('will release upon acceptance'), which limits reproducibility and verifiability of the claimed results, especially given that the closest competitor (MambaIC) had to be reimplemented by the authors.

The ablation table reports BD-rate deltas that do not exactly decompose additively (e.g., baseline -13.26 vs. CTA -15.21 and GPP -14.27, sum -15.91 combined), suggesting interaction effects that are not analyzed; also, ablations appear to be run only at the largest model scale.

strengths: Strong and convincing rate-distortion results: CMIC achieves the best reported BD-rate among compared methods (-15.91%/-21.34%/-17.58% vs VTM-21.0 on Kodak/Tecnick/CLIC), outperforming both SOTA Transformer-based (FTIC, S2CFormer, MLIC++) and Mamba-based (MambaVC, MambaIC) models.

Excellent efficiency-performance trade-off: 69.11M params, 2.39 TFLOPs, 0.405s latency, and 4.44GB peak memory substantially undercut MambaIC (157M params, 5.56 TFLOPs, 20GB memory) while achieving better RD performance; the single-scan design avoids the cost of multi-directional scanning.

Comprehensive and well-designed evaluation: comparisons against 10+ strong baselines with complexity tables; thorough ablations isolating CTP and GPP contributions, structural ablations (Conv block, 2D Mamba, attention-only, CAM-only), cluster number K, and cluster activation statistics.

Particularly valuable fairness checks in the appendix: swapping in the FTIC entropy model shows the transform network alone still beats FTIC (-15.67% vs -12.94% on Kodak), convincingly attributing gains to the proposed CAM module rather than the entropy model; entropy-model ablations show CAM is not beneficial everywhere, indicating honest reporting.

Good qualitative analysis: ERF visualizations demonstrating content-adaptive receptive fields, cluster visualizations showing semantic grouping (red doors, feathers, clouds), and training stability analysis across seeds addressing the non-differentiability concern.

Clear motivation: the two identified limitations of Mamba for images (content-agnostic scan and strict causality) are well-articulated, and the proposed mechanisms directly target them with low overhead (only ~4% inference latency increase, ~5% training time).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: both components are combinations of existing ideas — clustering-based token reordering has been explored in LIC (Zhang et al. 2024, acknowledged in A.2) and token permutation is established in diffusion/AR contexts (Hoogeboom et al.), while prompt injection into SSMs follows prior prompting work. The contribution is largely an engineering integration; the core insight that feature-space ordering helps linear-complexity sequence models is plausible but not deeply analyzed (e.g., no theoretical or empirical analysis of how reordering affects state retention or the state-space dynamics).

The causality-relaxation claim is oversold: adding a per-token prompt bias P to the output matrix C injects only cluster-identity-conditioned global statistics; the token still does not access features of subsequent tokens, so the strict causal information flow in the scan is unchanged. The mechanism is closer to conditional modulation than a genuine mitigation of sequential dependency, and the ablation gain from GPP (0.5-1.4%) is modest.

Margins over the strongest Mamba-based competitor (MambaIC) are moderate on Kodak (-2.36%) and CLIC (-2.17%), and the improvement over S2CFormer on Kodak is within the range often affected by BD-rate measurement variability; no error analysis or significance testing is provided.

Some important details affecting reproducibility are deferred or thin: the paper states code/checkpoints 'will be released later'; details such as how prompts interact with the hardware-efficient selective scan kernel, whether permutation breaks the causal masking of the SCCTX spatial context, and the exact integration of attention and CAM blocks across stages require careful reading of the appendix.

The entropy model contribution is secondary and explicitly not SOTA; readers seeking a unified methodological contribution may find the paper's value concentrated in one module (CAM), with the rest being a competent but standard LIC system (window attention + SCCTX variant).

Evaluation is limited to PSNR/MS-SSIM on standard test sets; no perceptual metric (LPIPS) or rate-distortion-perception analysis, and no evaluation under content distribution shift beyond CLIC professional.

strengths: Strong empirical results: consistent BD-rate gains over VTM-21.0 and prior Mamba-based LIC models (MambaVC, MambaIC) across Kodak, Tecnick, and CLIC, with favorable complexity (fewer parameters/FLOPs than MambaIC).

Comprehensive ablation studies (Table 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8) that isolate the contribution of Content-Adaptive Token Permutation and Global-Prior Prompting, and comparisons with alternative block structures (Conv, 2D Mamba, attention-only).
Interesting analyses, including Effective Receptive Field visualizations showing content-adaptive behavior, cluster activation statistics, and training-stability curves across seeds.
The codebook-based clustering with EMA updates is a reasonable engineering solution to the instability of per-sample online K-Means, with low parameter overhead and deterministic inference.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: token reordering/clustering for compression was already explored (Zhang et al., 2024; contextual clustering), Mamba-based LIC already exists (MambaVC, MambaIC), and the overall architecture (window attention + SSM blocks, SCCTX-based entropy model) closely follows prior work (Liu et al., 2023; He et al., 2022; FTIC). The core contribution is largely a combination of existing ideas applied to Mamba, and the direct head-to-head comparison with Zhang et al. (2024) is relegated to the appendix rather than the main table.

The central claim that Global-Prior Prompting 'overcomes the sequential dependency' or 'relaxes strict causality' is overstated and technically weakly supported. Injecting P = ΓU into the output matrix C merely adds a static, cluster-identity-conditioned bias to outputs; it does not propagate information from subsequent tokens, so the causal structure of the scan is fundamentally unchanged. The claim conflates a global conditioning signal with genuine non-causal context, and no analysis (e.g., information-flow tests, comparisons with truly bidirectional scans under matched cost) substantiates the causality-mitigation narrative.

Attribution of gains is unclear. CTP and GPP together contribute only ~2.7-3.6% BD-rate (Table 2), while the full model achieves ~15.9%; the remainder stems from the overall recipe (window attention blocks, enhanced entropy model) borrowed from prior work. Although Table 4 helps, the framing implies CAM drives the SOTA numbers, which the evidence only partially supports.

Non-differentiability of clustering and sorting introduces biased gradients; the paper's treatment (Appendix A.8) is largely empirical and brief, with no theoretical discussion of the bias or its magnitude.

Reproducibility is limited: code and checkpoints are only promised ('will be released later'), and key details (e.g., exact sort implementation, hardware-aware scan compatibility with arbitrary permutations, entropy-model group counts) are deferred to an appendix that is not fully self-contained.

MS-SSIM evaluation omits the main Mamba-based competitors, and some BD-PSNR gains over the strongest Transformer baseline (FTIC) are small (~0.15-0.36 dB), which weakens the 'significant SOTA' narrative.

strengths: Strong empirical results: CMIC achieves state-of-the-art RD performance on Kodak, Tecnick, and CLIC (BD-rates of -15.91%, -21.34%, -17.58% vs. VTM-21.0), clearly outperforming both Mamba-based (MambaVC, MambaIC) and Transformer-based (FTIC, S2CFormer) competitors across all bitrates and datasets.

Excellent complexity-performance trade-off: the model is substantially cheaper than competing Mamba-based models (56% fewer params, 57% fewer FLOPs, 39% lower latency, 78% less memory than MambaIC), making the contribution practically relevant, not just a leaderboard chase.

Comprehensive and convincing ablations: component-wise ablations (Tab. 2), structure ablations vs. Conv/2D-Mamba/attention variants (Tab. 4), cluster number K (Tab. 6), throughput overhead (Tab. 3), and—particularly commendable—entropy-model ablations (Tab. 7-8) showing that gains come from the transform rather than a stronger entropy model (CMIC still beats FTIC with the same T-CA entropy model).

Good qualitative analysis: ERF visualizations, per-image content-adaptive ERFs, cluster mask visualizations, and training-stability curves across seeds substantiate the claimed content-adaptivity and stability of the non-differentiable clustering.

Clear writing and well-motivated problem framing: the two identified limitations of vanilla Mamba for compression (rigid content-agnostic scan, strict causality) are well articulated, and the appendix (A.2, A.8-A.10) anticipates reviewer questions on the related clustering-based method (Zhang et al., 2024) and design choices.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the two proposed mechanisms are relatively simple. Token reordering via clustering-based grouping has a clear precedent in Zhang et al. (2024) (differentiated mainly by codebook-based vs. pooled centroids), and the codebook clustering with EMA updates is essentially VQ-VAE/K-Means machinery. The 'Global-Prior Prompting' amounts to adding a per-token vector P = ΓU to the output projection C—a modest architectural modification.

The causality-mitigation claim is overclaimed. Injecting P into C modulates the read-out per token but does not propagate information from subsequent tokens into a token's hidden state; early tokens in the scan still cannot access later content. The prompt provides sample-level, not truly non-causal, context, and the paper does not rigorously analyze what information actually flows or quantify how much causality is 'relaxed'.

Theoretical treatment of the non-differentiable clustering/permutation is thin. The authors acknowledge biased gradients but offer only empirical stability evidence; no analysis of the biased-gradient bias-variance trade-off, straight-through variants, or comparison to differentiable clustering alternatives.

Gains over the strongest Mamba baseline (MambaIC) are moderate (-2.17% to -6.48% BD-rate), so the incremental contribution over very recent work is not large, and the improvement over the clustered-reordering prior (Zhang et al.) is partly attributable to the underlying Mamba architecture rather than the clustering innovation alone.

Reproducibility concerns: code and checkpoints are only promised ('will be released later'); no MS-SSIM comparison against MambaVC/MambaIC; hardware/software details for latency measurements are underspecified (e.g., whether selective-scan kernels are the same across compared methods).
